extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers (wartime public); journalists; government/industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-item newspaper page reporting wartime government orders, industrial production changes, labor/occupational deferments, and commentary on journalistic duties during war. Contains Associated Press news dispatches and government directives relevant to production and civil policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective Service occupational deferment list
rubrics_metrics.description: Local boards were given a list of thirty-five occupations in the production of communication equipment to guide them in considering occupational deferment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equipment covered: "radios and radio equipment, radar, telephone and telegraph equipment, television and signaling apparatus." Officials emphasized that the list covers present activities in the project and that in classifying registrants they should "consider skill and qualification." The announcement lists specific job titles (e.g., all-around boring-mill operator, chemist, all-around machinist, radio crystal engineer, tester and adjuster, tool maker, personnel manager, production manager, maintenance mechanic, metallurgist, gage inspector, radio/grid and radar inspector, defective radio and radar equipment repairman, machine-tool setup man, etc.). It was noted that "all [those] listed require 'six months of training and pre-'" (i.e., six months of training and prequalification).

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB newsprint production freeze
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Production Board froze production at every American mill at a rate equal to the mill's average from April 1 to September 30, 1942, inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The freeze was described as "preliminary to an international concentration of production." It produced an estimated 5.15 percent domestic reduction and was expected to lead to further curtailments and concentration in 'nucleus' mills to operate at or near capacity. Exceptions and administrative procedures: owners of multiple mills may submit voluntary concentration plans (subject to approval by WPB's director general for Operations); an exception exists for 'machine' mills that have only one machine (see separate exception). The order also noted that "unrestricted production of six paper products is permitted to continue."

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-machine mill exception (keep machine busy)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception permits a mill equipped with only one machine to continue production to 'keep the machine busy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a mill may produce provided it keeps the machine busy (stated as '120 hours' in a calendar week) and is eligible for an exception that would otherwise be denied to larger multi-machine mills. Plans to combine production among mills (for owners of more than one mill) are allowed but require approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB priority delivery restriction for iron and steel products
rubrics_metrics.description: Warehouses were directed that no orders are to be filled on priorities rated lower than AA-5 for iron and steel products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously deliveries had been permitted on A-1-A orders or higher; the new rule tightened that to AA-5. The same restriction was applied to warehouses dealing in brass, mill and wire steel products. Exceptions permit deliveries for essential repairs and maintenance of alloy iron and alloy steel on ratings of A-1-K or higher, but such deliveries are limited to the warehouse's quota for alloy and tool steels and five percent of the quota for other iron and steel products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leather set-aside requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sole leather tanners and converters were ordered to set aside fifteen percent of their manufacturer's type sole leather production during November.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WPB order continued a percentage that 'has been allowed since August.' This is a conservation/allocation directive intended to reserve leather for priority uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnesium control extension (order M-2-B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control over the country's magnesium supply was continued by extending WPB order M-2-B from October 31 to December 31.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A straight extension of an existing control order to maintain government management of a strategic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance deliveries of canned fruits and vegetables
rubrics_metrics.description: The WPB authorized delivery of canned fruits and vegetables in advance of quota dates to relieve warehousing and financial hardship for some canners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance delivery is permitted only upon agreement by wholesalers, jobbers and retailers not to sell the goods in advance of quota dates. The order was said not to affect consumer supply but to permit earlier movement within the distribution chain under the stated restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sugar conservation order extension (M-98)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservation order M-98 controlling the distribution of raw sugar was extended indefinitely; it had been due to expire December 15.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls allocation of raw sugar among refineries and regions (e.g., Louisiana sugar moving to Southern refineries), as part of rationing/conservation efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery Tunnel halt and revocation order
rubrics_metrics.description: The WPB ordered an immediate stoppage of Battery Tunnel construction; prior limited construction permission (using materials on hand at the date of the original revocation) was revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order was described as 'necessary and appropriate in the public interest and . . . the national defense.' New York City Tunnel Authority could not continue limited construction beyond the permitted scope; it could use available materials and equipment already on hand only under limited conditions, but further maintenance or new work required WPB approval. Rationale: 'vast quantities of metal and other critical materials . . . are needed . . . in the manufacture of weapons and munitions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: OPA cigarette and cigar excise tax pass-through rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Price Administration announced that new federal excise taxes on cigarettes and cigars (and other taxable items) may be passed on to consumers, with specific rounding rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For cigarettes the new tax will add one-half cent per package; if the fraction is a half-cent or larger the seller may pass it on; if fractions are less than one-half cent the seller must absorb the tax. OPA warned manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers they must pass on 'no more than the exact amount of the increased tax' and must not compute mark-up on the tax. A forthcoming cigar regulation will allow an approximate 20 percent increase to consumers, including allowances for increased labor and raw material costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB technical development / idea-gathering program for ordnance
rubrics_metrics.description: A program to solicit and evaluate civilian technical ideas for redesigning and improving weapons was established, with a multi-step process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlined steps: 1) suggestion unit defines methods/ideas desired and writes functional specifications; 2) specifications and illustrations published in WPB News and distributed widely; 3) private engineers/technicians decide if they can contribute, work up plans and submit them to the WPB technical development section; 4) ordnance experts evaluate suggestions and adopt practicable ideas. The Chicago technical development section funnels ideas to experts of twenty-two cooperating technical societies; less than 1% of ideas were 'cranks or screwballs' in the initial sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB millwork industry survey and order classification
rubrics_metrics.description: WPB began a survey of the millwork industry to determine use of existing capacity for direct war requirements and whether facilities could be better utilized by concentration of war orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The survey aims to determine if plant facilities may be concentrated in strategically located areas. WPB officials indicated that 'the time is near when there will be only two classes of orders—those for direct war use and those for civilian requirement.' The order noted critical manpower shortages causing delays (estimated 20 to 120 days) and an overall deficit of about 14% of normal manpower in the industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB code of building standards and private builder priority
rubrics_metrics.description: WPB issued a code of building standards and stated that priority would again be given private builders upon completion of an overall review of materials, supplies and the need for additional sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The code was intended to regulate materials and supply priority for private home building within the wartime allocation regime. WPB officials said priority aid would be restored to private builders only after a comprehensive review.

rubrics_metrics.name: WPB limited exception quotas for essential alloy/tool steel deliveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliveries for essential repairs and maintenance of alloy iron and alloy steel are permitted on ratings of A-1-K or higher but are limited in quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such deliveries are confined to the warehouse's quota for alloy and tool steels, and five percent of the quota for other iron and steel products — a quota-based exception within the AA-5 priority framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic duty and restraint in wartime (Felix Belair)
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalist's professional duty is to obtain and publish every fact possible with reasonable promptitude, but wartime reporting requires compromises to protect security, morale and public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belair argued a 'series of compromises' is necessary: journalists must reveal facts and expose inefficiency but also refrain from publishing details whose disclosure would endanger security, health or public interest. He warned against withholding so much as to erode public confidence, and characterized wartime journalism as having a 'dual job'—informing the public while considering national security and morale consequences.
